section.title: Warning examples
section.p: Continuity gave us two promises: the Intermediate Value Theorem ensures a continuous graph cannot skip a height, and the Extreme Value Theorem ensures a continuous function on a closed bounded interval reaches an absolute maximum and minimum.

Those promises are strong because their hypotheses are strong. If we remove a hypothesis, the conclusion may fail. This section gathers the warnings in one place to prevent illegal applications of theorems.

subsection.title: A function with no limit at a jump
subsection.p: A two-sided limit needs one single target; a jump provides two distinct targets.

example.title: No two-sided limit at a jump

statement.p: As x\to 0^-, J(x)\to 0, while as x\to 0^+, J(x)\to 1. Because the one-sided limits disagree, \lim_{x\to 0}J(x) does not exist.

figure.caption: A jump creates two different one-sided limits, so the two-sided limit fails.

subsection.title: A limit that is infinite, not finite
subsection.p: A limit fails in a different way when values do not settle near any finite number.

example.title: Infinite divergence is not a finite limit

statement.p: Consider f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2} for x\neq 0. As x\to 0, x^2\to 0^+, so the values explode beyond every fixed bound.
We write \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x^2}=\infty, but this means unbounded growth, not that a finite limit L\in\mathbb{R} exists.

figure.caption: The values of 1/x^2 grow without bound near 0. This is infinite behavior, not a finite limit.

subsection.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem fails without continuity

statement.p: Define S(x)=\begin{cases}0, \amp x\lt 0, \\ 2, \amp x\ge 0.\end{cases} On [-1,1], S(-1)=0 and S(1)=2. The intermediate value N=1 is never attained because S is discontinuous at 0.

figure.caption: Without continuity, a function can jump over an intermediate value.

subsection.title: The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an open interval

statement.p: Consider f(x)=x on the open interval (0,1). The function is continuous at every point in (0,1), but values approach 0 and 1 without ever reaching them. Hence f has neither an absolute maximum nor an absolute minimum on (0,1).

figure.caption: On (0,1), the function f(x)=x approaches its lowest and highest possible values but never reaches them.

subsection.title: The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an unbounded interval

example.title: Unbounded interval allows escape to infinity

statement.p: Consider f(x)=x on [0,\infty). It achieves a minimum f(0)=0, but no maximum exists because f(x+1)\gt f(x) for all x.
Similarly, the cooling model T(t)=70+\frac{90}{t+1} on [0,\infty) attains its maximum T(0)=160 but never reaches its infimum 70 at any finite time t.

subsection.title: A map of the warnings

table.title: Summary of conditions, hypotheses, and failure modes

subsection.p: A theorem is a logical contract: when all hypotheses are met, the conclusion is guaranteed; when any hypothesis is violated, guarantees vanish. The next section explores limiting processes where the index is a whole number n: sequences.
